lead: A latch stores one bit in a feedback loop that is open for part of the clock: while open, the output follows the input; while closed, it holds. Two latches on opposite clock phases make an edge-triggered register, the store behind every pipeline stage, counter and shift register. A static latch keeps its bit in a regenerating loop for as long as power is on. A dynamic latch keeps it as charge on a capacitance, which is smaller and faster but leaks away, so the clock must keep running.
prereq: You need: transmission gates (see pass transistor logic and transmission gates), the inverter switching voltage VM (see CMOS inverter DC characteristics) and the 2:1 multiplexer of Chapter 4.5.

blocks.text: Two inverters connected in a ring are bistable. Their two transfer curves, drawn on one set of axes, cross at three points. The points near 0 V and V<sub>DD</sub> are stable, because each inverter's gain is below 1 there and a small disturbance dies away. The middle point, with both nodes at the switching voltage V<sub>M</sub>, is metastable: the loop gain is above 1, so any noise grows until the loop falls to 0 or 1. Writing a latch means forcing the loop past V<sub>M</sub>; data changing too close to the clock edge can leave it hanging near V<sub>M</sub>, which is metastability.

The SR latch builds the loop from two cross-coupled NOR gates: S = 1 sets Q = 1, R = 1 resets it, S = R = 0 holds, and S = R = 1 is not allowed (both outputs go to 0 and the release is a race). NAND gates give the same latch with active-low inputs.

The gated D latch removes the forbidden input. In CMOS it is built as a multiplexer: Q = CLK·D + CLK′·Q. While CLK = 1 the latch is transparent and Q follows D; while CLK = 0 the multiplexer selects the feedback path and the loop holds the last value. A positive latch (transparent when CLK = 1) uses two transmission gates and two inverters: one gate admits D, the other closes the inverter loop on the opposite clock phase. The 6T SRAM cell keeps its bit in the same cross-coupled inverter loop but writes it through access transistors (Chapter 4.9).

sections.h3: Master-slave register, timing and shift registers

blocks.text: A master-slave register is a negative latch (the master) followed by a positive latch (the slave). While CLK = 0 the master is transparent and follows D; the slave is opaque and holds the old output. At the rising edge the master closes and keeps the value D had just before the edge, and the slave opens and copies it to Q. While CLK = 1 the master is closed, so the slave has nothing new to pass. Q therefore changes once per period, just after the rising edge: the pair is a rising-edge-triggered register. Swapping the two latches gives a falling-edge register.

Three timing numbers describe a register. Setup time tsu: D must be stable this long before the edge. Hold time th: D must stay stable this long after it. Clock-to-Q delay tcq: the time from the edge to a valid Q. For a path through logic of delay tcomb to the next register (Chapter 4.8 works a full example with skew):
Here the setup check uses the longest path; setup slack = T − t<sub>cq</sub> − t<sub>comb,max</sub> − t<sub>su</sub> ≥ 0, and f<sub>max</sub> = 1 ÷ T<sub>min</sub>.

Here the hold check uses the shortest path (and, strictly, the fastest clock-to-Q delay). T does not appear, so slowing the clock cannot fix a hold failure. Clock skew and jitter enter both checks; Chapter 4.8 adds them.

A register is n flip-flops sharing one clock. A shift register chains them: Q of stage i drives D of stage i + 1, so each clock edge moves every bit one place. Read all stages at once and it is a serial-in parallel-out converter (worked example); load the stages in parallel and shift out, and it is parallel-in serial-out. This works only because the stages are edge-triggered: transparent latches on one clock would let a bit race through several stages.

sections.h3: Dynamic latches and registers: C²MOS and TSPC

blocks.text: A dynamic latch drops the feedback loop and keeps the bit as charge on the gate capacitance of the next inverter. The dynamic transmission-gate register is the simplest: transmission gate, inverter, transmission gate, inverter, eight transistors in all. While CLK = 0 the first gate is on and the master node follows D; at the rising edge it turns off and the node holds its charge, while the second gate passes the value on to the output inverter. It is small and fast, but if CLK and CLK′ overlap (both briefly 1, or both 0) the two gates conduct together and D can race through to Q.

The C<sup>2</sup>MOS register (clocked CMOS) removes that risk. Each transmission gate and inverter becomes one clocked inverter: two pMOS in series above the output and two nMOS in series below it, with the clock on one transistor of each pair. The master is clocked by CLK′ and the slave by CLK. During a 0-0 clock overlap only the pull-up halves of the two stages can conduct; during a 1-1 overlap only the pull-down halves. Because both stages invert, a value passing through both needs a pull-up in one stage and a pull-down in the other, and an overlap only ever turns on the same half in both. So the register is insensitive to clock overlap, as long as the clock edges are sharp.

The true single-phase clock register (TSPC) uses only CLK, so there is no CLK′ to generate, route or skew. A TSPC latch is two cascaded clocked inverter stages driven by CLK alone: a positive latch is transparent while CLK is high and a negative latch while it is low. A negative latch followed by a positive latch is a rising-edge register. It is compact and fast, and common in high-speed frequency dividers.

Static or dynamic? A static loop replaces any charge lost to leakage, so the bit survives with the clock stopped. A dynamic node only holds charge, which leaks away, so the clock must come back before the node voltage droops by more than the allowed ΔV. Treating the whole period as hold time:

blocks.where: I<sub>leak</sub> is the leakage current in A, C the storage capacitance in F, ΔV the allowed droop in V and f<sub>min</sub> the lowest safe clock frequency in Hz. A static latch has no f<sub>min</sub>: it works down to DC.

examples.question: A 4-bit serial-in parallel-out shift register (stages Q₀ → Q₁ → Q₂ → Q₃, rising-edge triggered) starts at Q₀Q₁Q₂Q₃ = 0000. The serial input D<sub>in</sub> feeds Q₀ and is 1, 0, 1, 1 at clock edges 1 to 4. Give the stage contents after every edge and the 4-bit word read in parallel after edge 4.
steps: At each edge, every stage takes the old value of the stage before it: Q₃ ← Q₂, Q₂ ← Q₁, Q₁ ← Q₀, Q₀ ← D<sub>in</sub>, all at the same instant.
The first bit sent is now in Q₃ and the last in Q₀. Reading Q₃Q₂Q₁Q₀ gives 1011, the bits in the order they were sent.
examples.answer: After four edges Q₀Q₁Q₂Q₃ = 1101, so the parallel word Q₃Q₂Q₁Q₀ = 1011: four serial bits have become one 4-bit word.

traps: A single gated D latch is level-sensitive, not edge-triggered. Only the master-slave pair, or another edge circuit, is a register.
Setup uses the longest path and contains T; hold uses the shortest path and has no T. Slowing the clock fixes setup, not hold.

A dynamic latch has a minimum clock frequency; a static latch works down to DC. A dynamic transmission-gate register also fails on clock overlap, which C<sup>2</sup>MOS and TSPC are designed to survive.
In a shift register the first bit sent ends up in the last stage.

quiz.q: Define setup time t<sub>su</sub> and hold time t<sub>h</sub> for a flip-flop.
quiz.a: t<sub>su</sub> is the time data must be stable before the capturing clock edge. t<sub>h</sub> is the time data must remain stable after the edge.

quiz.q: Why is a gated D latch not called edge-triggered?
quiz.a: It is transparent for the whole enable level. While EN=1, any D change reaches Q; it does not sample only at an edge.

quiz.q: A hold check fails on a short path. Can you fix it by lowering the clock frequency? Explain.
quiz.a: No. Hold compares data arrival after the edge with t<sub>h</sub>; T cancels out. Add delay in the short path, increase t<sub>cq,</sub> or reduce t<sub>h</sub>.

quiz.q: A dynamic latch has C = 20 fF, leakage I<sub>leak</sub> = 2 nA and allowed droop ΔV = 0.10 V. Find the minimum clock frequency.
What does TSPC stand for, and what is its main advantage?
quiz.a: True single-phase clock. Its latches and registers need only CLK, not CLK and CLK′, so no complementary clock has to be generated or kept free of skew.

quiz.q: Why is the C²MOS register insensitive to clock overlap when the dynamic transmission-gate register is not?
quiz.a: In the transmission-gate register both gates conduct during an overlap, so D can race to Q. In C<sup>2</sup>MOS a 0-0 overlap turns on only the pull-up halves and a 1-1 overlap only the pull-down halves. Since both stages invert, a value passing both needs a pull-up in one and a pull-down in the other, which no overlap provides, so it cannot race through, provided the clock edges are sharp.

beyond: Not for the exam. High-speed designs use pulsed latches and time borrowing on critical paths, and sense-amplifier flip-flops in fast links. Search next for "pulsed latch" and "time borrowing".
